subject: Chemistry
title: Covalent Bonds: Sharing Electrons
description: A micro-lesson that makes Covalent Bonds: Sharing Electrons usable.

hook.text: Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons to form H₂. Neither gains nor loses—they share. That's a covalent bond.

buildup.text: Each hydrogen has one electron but wants two to fill its shell. Sharing gives both atoms a full outer shell.

discovery.text: The shared electrons create a region of negative charge between the nuclei, pulling them together.

twist.text: Double bonds share four electrons (like O₂). Triple bonds share six (like N₂). More sharing means shorter, stronger bonds.

climax.text: Diamond is pure carbon with four covalent bonds per atom. This 3D network makes it the hardest natural material.

punchline.text: Sharing electrons, both atoms benefit. Cooperation at the atomic level.

quiz.question: What makes diamond so hard?
options: Every carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in a rigid 3D network
Diamond contains metallic bonds between carbon atoms
Diamond's atoms are compressed by extreme pressure underground

details.summary: Covalent bonds form when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons, creating a stable electron configuration for both. This sharing produces discrete molecules with definite shapes and makes possible the enormous diversity of organic chemistry and biological molecules.
details.whyItMatters: Covalent bonding underlies all of organic chemistry, biochemistry, and polymer science. Every protein, every drug, and every plastic depends on covalent bonds between atoms.
takeaways: Atoms share electron pairs to achieve stable configurations
Single, double, and triple bonds share one, two, or three pairs
Molecular shape depends on electron pair geometry around atoms

faq.question: What determines whether a bond is single, double, or triple?
faq.answer: The number of shared electron pairs determines bond order. Carbon-carbon bonds can be single, double, or triple depending on how many electrons each carbon needs to share. Higher bond orders mean shorter, stronger bonds with different chemical reactivity.

faq.question: How do polar covalent bonds differ from nonpolar covalent bonds?
faq.answer: In nonpolar bonds, electrons are shared equally because both atoms have similar electronegativity. In polar bonds, one atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly, creating partial positive and negative ends. Water's O-H bonds are polar; molecular oxygen's O-O bond is nonpolar.
